title: One process sends far more data than it ever has, while the network stays healthy

problem.summary: A process starts pushing bulk data out of the host. Nothing is broken: no packets are lost, no retransmissions, latency is normal, and every service still answers. That is what makes it hard. Every other network fault in this library is about IMPAIRMENT - packets dropped, delay added - and this one is the opposite: the network works perfectly and is being used heavily. The question is whether a blueprint can separate unusual traffic from merely heavy traffic, and the answer turns on measuring the process that arrived rather than the host total.
symptoms: outbound traffic well above normal with no errors anywhere
no packet loss and no retransmission
services still answer at normal latency
the host looks healthy on every saturation measure

discriminators.signal: bytes per second gained by a process that was barely sending before, from net_dev_queue
discriminators.this_problem: one process arrives sending ~81 MB/s it was not sending before
discriminators.not_this_problem: no other fault family gains more than 3.6 MB/s on either application
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED across 303 runs covering ALL 27 fault families on two applications. The fault gains 8.11e7 bytes/s on both; the highest gain in any other family is 1.98e6 (Sock Shop) and 3.64e6 (Train Ticket). A 22x gap. 10 of 10 confirmed runs separated, no false fire. See evidence/data-exfiltration_separation.json

discriminators.signal: host outbound bytes, incident against baseline
discriminators.this_problem: rises 6.2x on one application and 24.9x on the other, for the same absolute transfer
discriminators.not_this_problem: overlaps with other families on one of the two applications, so it cannot be used
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED and RETRACTED as a discriminator. The host-wide ratio separates cleanly on Sock Shop and fails on Train Ticket, because the applications carry different baseline traffic - Sock Shop already moves ~12.8 MB/s, so the same absolute transfer reads 6.2x there and 24.9x on Train Ticket. Recorded because it is the obvious measure to reach for and it does not transfer. See evidence/data-exfiltration_separation.json

MEASURED on the network sweep: a degraded path retransmits 18.5-60.7% of segments while this fault leaves retransmission flat. Used to rule OUT the network blueprint rather than to rule this one in - heavy traffic and a losing path look alike on volume and opposite on loss. See evidence/data-exfiltration_separation.json

reproduction.system: Sock Shop or Train Ticket on Ubuntu 24.04, LTTng 2.15, Docker 27+, single GCP n2 VM
harness_only: A benign simulation on an isolated VM: generated bytes sent to a listener inside the same container at a steady rate. Nothing leaves the host, no real data is read, and no external address is contacted. What it reproduces is the SHAPE of bulk egress, not an actual exfiltration.

collection_order.why_these: MEASURED BASIS. net_dev_queue carries the byte count, the interface, the protocol and ports, AND the process that was on-CPU when the buffer was queued, which is what makes per-process attribution possible at all. One event type decides this blueprint. Loss and retransmission events are not needed to fire it - they are needed only to rule out the network blueprint, and the pack already carries them.

processing.step: stage the stored kernel trace for reading
processing.expect: a CTF directory the trace reader can open

processing.step: measure bytes sent per process, both windows, and report the newcomer
processing.expect: bytes per second per process in each window, and the process whose rate rose most

processing.step: confirm the path is healthy, so heavy traffic is not mistaken for a losing path
processing.expect: retransmission percentage per interface; this fault leaves it flat

processing.step: combine into the verdict and its artifacts
processing.expect: a verdict naming the sending process, or an explicit non-fire with the reason

outputs.contains: verdict, the sending process, bytes per second gained, the destination ports it used, and the retransmission rate that rules out a network fault
outbound bytes per second per process, baseline against incident
which process started sending, how much, and why this is heavy traffic rather than a degraded path
map the process to its container and its destination, then decide whether the transfer is expected before throttling or blocking it

verdict_when: a process gains more than 3.6 MB per second of outbound traffic over its baseline
that process was sending little or nothing before
retransmission stays low, so the path is healthy rather than losing packets

rule_out.when: retransmission is high. A losing path also moves bytes, but it moves the SAME bytes repeatedly. Volume alone cannot tell the two apart; loss can.
retransmission is very high and one container is at its memory limit. A capped container cannot drain its sockets, which produces heavy retransmission that looks like traffic.
no process gains meaningful outbound volume, even if the host total looks raised. The host total is application-specific - see the retracted discriminator.

decision.root_cause_is: a process sending bulk data it does not normally send, identified by its command name and destination port

apply_when: outbound traffic is well above normal
no errors, no loss, and normal latency
per-process network attribution is available from the kernel trace
do_not_apply_when: packets are being lost or retransmitted heavily
a container is at its memory limit
applicability.cheap_precheck: sum net_dev_queue bytes per process in each window. If no single process gained more than a few MB per second, this blueprint does not apply.

capabilities_required.why: the stored kernel trace must be readable
the deciding signal: bytes per second per process, and who arrived
not to fire the rule, but to rule out a degraded path, which also moves bytes

stopping_conditions.conclude: one process gained tens of MB per second of outbound traffic it was not sending before, with the path healthy
stopping_conditions.stop_and_switch: retransmission high -> network-path-degradation; retransmission very high with a container at its memory limit -> service-memory-cap
stopping_conditions.stop_insufficient: net_dev_queue was not recorded, so egress cannot be attributed -> request it and re-run. Do NOT fall back to the host outbound total, which was measured to separate on one application only.

evidence_sufficiency.if_below_floor: name the unresolved question, pick the ONE additional capability that would settle it, check it against the overhead budget, and request it.
evidence_sufficiency.report_when_stuck: if the floor is still not met after the allowed rounds, report the best-supported hypothesis, its confidence, and precisely what evidence is missing - never present a guess as a diagnosis

sibling_causes: a backup or replication job running at the wrong time
a debug dump or profiler shipping data off-host
taxonomy.note: The deciding fact is that a process started sending volume it does not normally send. That is agnostic to intent: the same signature covers a runaway backup and a malicious transfer, and the blueprint deliberately does not try to tell them apart. Deciding whether the transfer is legitimate is a question for the operator, not the trace.

preconditions: net_dev_queue is collectable or already collected
per-process attribution is acceptable as approximate - the event is attributed to whatever was on-CPU when the buffer was queued, not strictly to the socket owner

historical_effectiveness.note: 10 labelled data_exfiltration runs across two applications, separated from 293 runs of the other 26 families with a 22x gap between the lowest positive (8.11e7 bytes/s) and the highest negative (3.64e6). Both applications agree to within 0.3%.

provenance.authored_by: measured across all 303 v2 runs and all 27 fault families, both applications
provenance.notes: The recipe registered a doubt about itself before any data existed: 'this asks whether a blueprint can separate UNUSUAL traffic from HEAVY traffic, and the honest answer may be not from volume alone'. Measured, volume alone DOES separate it - with a 22x margin on both applications - provided the volume is attributed to the process that arrived rather than summed over the host. The host total is exactly the measure the doubt applies to: it separates on Sock Shop and fails on Train Ticket, because the two applications carry different baseline traffic. So the doubt was right about the signal it had in mind and wrong about the fault. Both halves are recorded. The threshold was placed against the other families' highest value, never fitted to the positives.
